# tabular-center

**State machines whose declaration *is* the transition matrix** -- for Rust,
Kotlin and Swift, held to one behaviour by a shared conformance suite.

You write the matrix. Every cell is one word, or a call to code you write. The
compiler refuses a machine with a hole in it.

```rust
transition_matrix! {
    machine Timer;
    context Ctx;
    state   State;
    action  Action;
    effects Effect { StartClock, StopClock { reason: Reason } }
    initial Idle;

    states  { Idle, Running { since: u64 }, Done }
    actions { Start, Tick { now: u64 }, Cancel }

    //            Start                                  Tick     Cancel
    Idle    => [  HANDLE,                                IGNORE,  IGNORE                                  ];
    Running => [  IGNORE,                                HANDLE,  GO!(Idle, StopClock { reason: Reason::Cancelled }) ];
    Done    => [  GO!(Running { since: 0 }, StartClock), IGNORE,  IGNORE                                  ];
}
```

<sub>From [`tabular-center-rust/examples/02-timer/src/machine.tb.rs`](https://github.com/tabula-center/tabular-center/blob/main/tabular-center-rust/examples/02-timer/src/machine.tb.rs).</sub>

That is the whole behaviour of a three-state timer. Five of its nine cells are
decided right there -- `IGNORE`, or `GO!` to a state with an effect -- and cost
nothing more. Two are `HANDLE`: those, and only those, become methods you
implement, each receiving its state and action already narrowed to concrete
types. Forget one and the build fails naming it.

## The one guarantee

> Every cell of the state × action matrix is a required member.
> **An incomplete machine does not compile.**

Not pattern-match exhaustiveness, which `else`, `default:` and `_` defeat.
Not purity, which Kotlin and Swift cannot enforce. The oldest mechanism in all
three languages: *you declared a required member and did not implement it.*
States, actions **and effects** are generated sum types, so adding an effect
breaks every handler's build the same way adding a state breaks every matrix.

## Concise at the size that matters

The Timer is small on purpose. Here is a real order lifecycle, 8 states by 12
actions:

```rust
transition_matrix! {
    machine Order;
    context Ctx;
    state   State;
    action  Action;
    effects Effect {
        RequestPayment, ReleaseHold, NotifyExpired, ChargeCard,
        NotifyFailure, SchedulePickup, NotifyShipped, IssueRefund, NotifyDelivered
    }
    initial Draft;

    states {
        Draft, AwaitingPayment, PaymentFailed { code: u32 }, Paid,
        Preparing, Shipped { tracking: u64 }, Delivered, Cancelled
    }
    actions {
        AddItem, RemoveItem, Submit, PaidOk, PaidFail { code: u32 }, Retry,
        Cancel, Prepare, Ship { tracking: u64 }, Deliver, Refund, Expire
    }

    //                    AddItem  RemoveItem  Submit                                  PaidOk                     PaidFail  Retry   Cancel                          Prepare                       Ship                                   Deliver                                    Refund  Expire
    Draft           => [  HANDLE,  HANDLE,     GO!(AwaitingPayment, RequestPayment),   IGNORE,                    IGNORE,   IGNORE, GO!(Cancelled),                 IGNORE,                       IGNORE,                                IGNORE,                                    IGNORE, GO!(Cancelled, NotifyExpired) ];
    AwaitingPayment => [  IGNORE,  IGNORE,     IGNORE,                                 GO!(Paid, ChargeCard),     HANDLE,   IGNORE, GO!(Cancelled, ReleaseHold),    IGNORE,                       IGNORE,                                IGNORE,                                    IGNORE, GO!(Cancelled, ReleaseHold)   ];
    PaymentFailed   => [  IGNORE,  IGNORE,     IGNORE,                                 IGNORE,                    IGNORE,   HANDLE, GO!(Cancelled, ReleaseHold),    IGNORE,                       IGNORE,                                IGNORE,                                    IGNORE, GO!(Cancelled, ReleaseHold)   ];
    Paid            => [  IGNORE,  IGNORE,     IGNORE,                                 IGNORE,                    IGNORE,   IGNORE, GO!(Cancelled, IssueRefund),    GO!(Preparing, SchedulePickup), IGNORE,                               IGNORE,                                    GO!(Cancelled, IssueRefund), IGNORE ];
    Preparing       => [  IGNORE,  IGNORE,     IGNORE,                                 IGNORE,                    IGNORE,   IGNORE, HANDLE,                         IGNORE,                       HANDLE,                                IGNORE,                                    HANDLE, IGNORE ];
    Shipped         => [  IGNORE,  IGNORE,     IGNORE,                                 IGNORE,                    IGNORE,   IGNORE, IGNORE,                         IGNORE,                       IGNORE,                                GO!(Delivered, NotifyDelivered),           HANDLE, IGNORE ];
    Delivered       => [  IGNORE,  IGNORE,     IGNORE,                                 IGNORE,                    IGNORE,   IGNORE, IGNORE,                         IGNORE,                       IGNORE,                                IGNORE,                                    HANDLE, IGNORE ];
    Cancelled       => [  IGNORE,  IGNORE,     IGNORE,                                 IGNORE,                    IGNORE,   IGNORE, IGNORE,                         IGNORE,                       IGNORE,                                IGNORE,                                    IGNORE, IGNORE ];
}
```

<sub>From [`tabular-center-rust/tabular-center/tests/scale.rs`](https://github.com/tabula-center/tabular-center/blob/main/tabular-center-rust/tabular-center/tests/scale.rs).</sub>

| | |
|---|---|
| cells | 96 |
| `IGNORE` | 75 (78%) |
| `GO!` | 12 |
| **methods you write** | **9** |

Measured, not estimated: `ninety_six_cells_cost_nine_implementations` in that
file asserts the 9. Eight lines declare 96 transitions, the grid stays
reviewable as a grid, and the 75 cells that do nothing cost one word each --
which is the only reason a machine this size is pleasant to write at all.

## Composition, checked by the same mechanism

A parent hands cells to a child written knowing nothing about it:

```rust
    //                 Credentials         StartOver           Logout
    LoggedOut  => [     DELEGATE!(auth),   DELEGATE!(auth),    IGNORE                    ];
    Active     => [     IGNORE,            IGNORE,             GO!(Banned, Audit)        ];
    Banned     => [     IGNORE,            IGNORE,             IGNORE                    ];
```

<sub>From [`tabular-center-rust/examples/04-login/src/session.tb.rs`](https://github.com/tabula-center/tabular-center/blob/main/tabular-center-rust/examples/04-login/src/session.tb.rs).</sub>

The parent's cell surface requires the child's, so a hole in the child is a
build error in the parent -- the same error as a hole in the parent itself.
No registration, no runtime check. It holds in all three languages, each with
a compile-fail fixture proving it, and through colors: a plain child composes
into an `async` or `suspend` parent; the reverse does not compile.

## Three languages, one behaviour

| | [Rust](rust) | [Kotlin](kotlin) | [Swift](swift) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Generator | `macro_rules!` -- no build step, no dependencies | KSP, from annotations | `TabulaCodegen` today; the `@Machine` macro is designed and pending |
| Runtime dependencies | none, `no_std` capable | none | none |
| Colors | `async` | `suspend`, receivers, any modifier | `async`, `throws`, attributes |
| Driver | blocking, non-reentrant mailbox | blocking and `suspend` | sync and `async`, `ObservableStore` |
| Introspection | `TABLE`, grid, Mermaid, DOT, lints, coverage | the same | the same |

The same fixtures in `spec/conformance/` are replayed by all three, and each
renders every fixture's grid, diagram, lints and coverage; a check diffs the
three and fails on a single differing byte. A semantic difference between the
languages is a red build, not a bug report.
